title: The Former Tyre Shop on Rua Oscar Freire Where Natura Began
dek: In 1970 Luiz Seabra gave skin consultations in a little São Paulo shop; four years later Natura closed it and sold through trained consultants instead.

story.event: Becoming a partner in a small cosmetics laboratory, running the Oscar Freire shop himself, then closing it for direct sales
story.summary: In 1969 Luiz Seabra, an economist who had run the administration of a small São Paulo cosmetics laboratory since 1966, became a partner in it and turned it into a maker and seller of its own products, named Natura months later. He served customers himself in a small shop on Rua Oscar Freire, opened in 1970 in a former tyre-repair garage; the years were financially hard, and in 1974 Natura closed the shop and moved to direct sales through trained consultants.
paragraphs: In 1970, in a narrow shop on Rua Oscar Freire in São Paulo that had once been a tyre-repair garage, Luiz Seabra, an economist in his late twenties, sat with customers and talked to them about their skin. The street was nearly empty then; he later remembered only a dry cleaner, a beautician on the corner of Haddock Lobo and a bakery run by a Finn. Natura's own history says Seabra served the customers himself, and that each early customer was given a white rose.

He had come to cosmetics sideways. The son of a seamstress, he started work at 15 and by 19 held a management post at Remington, the electric-shaver company. In 1966 he went to run the administration of a small cosmetics laboratory whose owner, a French aesthetician, treated clients nearby. There he learned about skin, and was, he said, scandalised by the industry's language: labels sold "anti-age" as a virtue, which he saw as a lie about women and time. In 1969, aged 27, he was invited to become a partner and turn the laboratory into a maker and seller of its own products. One company history says it began with $9,000 in cash and a handful of formulas by Jean-Pierre Berjeaut. Months later it was named Natura.

The shop taught him something he had not planned. Seeing customers one by one, he later said, showed him how much relationships mattered. It did not pay well. "They were difficult years," he told Exame in 1998; at times there was no money for the electricity bill. He also gave talks around Brazil. But one shop and his own voice could not grow: there were no franchises then, more shops meant outside investors, and ordinary retail would lose the personal consultation. His answer, he said, was to multiply the number of "Luizes".

In 1973 Natura opened a small factory in São Paulo, where seven people made about 600 units a month. In 1974 it closed the Oscar Freire shop and turned to direct sales: consultants trained to use a catalogue recommended treatments and kept 20 to 30 per cent. Some had been customers at the shop. By 1986, a company history records, Natura had 16,000 consultants.

quote.text: A man of smiling countenance sold honey, captivating the hearts of all by his pleasant manner. His customers were as numerous as flies around the sugar-cane—if he had sold poison people would have bought it for honey.
quote.locator: Chapter IV, "Concerning Humility", Story of the Honey-seller
quote.source_title: The Bustān of Sadi, tr. A. Hart Edwards, Project Gutenberg eBook #60471
quote.connection: Seabra found that customers trusted a warm consultation, and built Natura by multiplying it through thousands of others. Saadi's honey-seller is charming enough to sell poison as honey. A pleasant manner proves nothing about what is in the jar, and Saadi does not say what does.

reflection: The little shop on Oscar Freire was, by Seabra's own account, not a business that could last. It was where he learned what would: that people trusted a conversation more than a label. He kept the conversation and let the shop go.

Saadi's honey-seller is a fair warning beside that. Warmth persuades, and it can persuade people of the wrong thing. You are often the one in the room explaining what something does. It is worth asking, now and then, whether people are trusting the evidence or trusting you, and making sure the first could stand without the second.
invitation: Pick one claim you often make about your work and write the evidence for it in two lines. If you cannot, soften the claim the next time you say it.

cross_checks.claim: Seabra founded Natura in 1969 and it first traded from a small shop on Rua Oscar Freire
Seabra served customers himself, giving consultations in the shop
He worked at a small cosmetics laboratory from 1966 and was invited to become a partner in 1969
In 1974 Natura closed the shop and adopted direct sales
The shop could not sustain growth, so Seabra chose to train consultants

research_notes: Shop date: Natura's investor-relations timeline and its 2009 annual report say the Oscar Freire shop opened in 1970, the year after the 1969 founding; Brazil Journal and the International Directory of Company Histories (IDCH) imply the shop dates from the founding. The story opens in 1970 and keeps the founding in 1969. Seabra's job at founding: the IDCH says he was working as an economist at Remington (Sperry Rand) when he founded Natura; his own later accounts (Brazil Journal 2023, NeoFeed 2025) say he left Remington and had been managing a small cosmetics laboratory since 1966 (at 24), becoming a partner in 1969; the story follows his own account. The owner of that laboratory is described by Seabra only as a French aesthetician; the IDCH names Jean-Pierre Berjeaut as the source of the first formulas; the story does not say they are the same person. The $9,000 starting cash comes only from the IDCH and is attributed to 'one company history'. Consultant numbers: the IDCH gives 2,000 salespeople in the years after 1974 and 16,000 by 1986; the story uses the dated 1986 figure. Seabra's Brazilian interviews are in Portuguese and are paraphrased; the only direct quotation, 'They were difficult years', is the IDCH's English rendering of his 1998 remark to Exame, and 'Luizes' is his own word. The 2009 annual report PDF loads but its text is not machine-readable for the checker. The Saadi story is about temper and manner in selling; applied here by analogy.
